title: Monitor, Log, and Collect AI Security Telemetry
intro: Giving security operations the visibility AI systems need: collecting telemetry on prompts, completions, embeddings and retrieval, tool calls and API traffic; correlating AI events across SIEM, SOAR and threat intelligence pipelines; keeping logs tamper-evident and documenting them as evidence; masking personal data and secrets without blinding detection; and monitoring AI behaviour, performance drift and agent actions in real time.
objectives: Identify the AI telemetry to collect at the gateway, agent, retrieval, model and tool layers, joined by trace IDs
Correlate AI events in the SIEM, automate safe responses with SOAR, and use and share AI threat intelligence
Protect log integrity and completeness, and document AI logs as evidence with hashing and chain of custody
Apply privacy-preserving masking to AI telemetry while keeping it useful for detection and investigation
Monitor AI behaviour, performance drift, agent actions and resource use in real time, with automatic, reversible guards

sections.title: AI telemetry: what to collect, and where

blocks.title: What the SOC needs to see

scenes.title: What the SOC needs to see
scenes.sub: AI telemetry data and where to collect it
scenes.say: Security teams can only detect what they can see. AI systems create new kinds of activity, and traditional logs miss most of it. | This video covers the AI telemetry a security operations centre needs: prompts, completions, embeddings, tool calls and API traffic, and where to collect them.

scenes.title: Sources of AI telemetry

items.d: User text, files, images, system prompt version
What was blocked, flagged or masked

scenes.say: AI telemetry comes from six main sources. | Prompts and inputs: what users and applications send, including files and images, and which version of the system prompt was in use. | Completions and outputs: what the model returned, including refusals and structured outputs. | Embeddings and retrieval: the search queries a retrieval system ran, which documents came back, and their similarity scores. | Tool calls and agent steps: which tool an agent called, with what arguments, what came back, and who approved it. | API and gateway traffic: who called, from where, how often, how many tokens, and which errors occurred. | And guardrail decisions: what was blocked, flagged or masked, and by which policy.

scenes.title: Collection points along one request
scenes.say: Telemetry is collected at several points along a single request. The AI gateway sees identity, rate limits and data loss prevention decisions. | The orchestrator or agent framework sees the plan, each step and any human approvals. | The retrieval layer sees the queries it ran and the documents it returned. | Model serving sees the model version, token counts and latency. | Tools and APIs see the calls made on the model’s behalf, their results and errors. | Security analytics brings these together. The key is a shared trace identifier on every event, so analysts can follow one request from end to end.

scenes.title: Metadata or content?
rows: Prove what was said; tune detections
scenes.say: A key design decision is how much content to collect, as opposed to metadata. | Metadata covers who, when, which model, how many tokens and which decisions were made. Content is the text of prompts, outputs and documents. | Metadata is small and cheap to keep. Content is large and costly. | Metadata carries lower privacy risk, although it is still personal data. Content can hold personal data and secrets. | Metadata is enough to spot most patterns and anomalies. Content is needed to prove exactly what was said, and to tune detections. Most organisations collect metadata for everything, and content selectively.

scenes.title: Questions telemetry must answer
scenes.say: A good test of AI telemetry is whether it answers six questions during an investigation. | Who sent the request: which user, agent, key and source? | What answered it: which model, and which prompt and configuration versions? | What context was used: which documents and memories were retrieved? | What did the system do: which tools did it call, and with what effect? | What left the system: which outputs, messages or data went out? | And what did it cost, in tokens, compute and time?

items: Collect prompts, outputs, retrieval, tool calls, API traffic and guardrail decisions
Instrument the gateway, orchestrator, retrieval, serving and tools
Join events with one trace ID
Metadata for everything; content selectively and protected
scenes.say: To recap. | Collect telemetry on prompts, outputs, retrieval, tool calls, API traffic and guardrail decisions. | Instrument the gateway, the orchestrator, retrieval, model serving and tools. | Join every event with a shared trace identifier. | And collect metadata for everything, but content selectively, with strong protection.

blocks.md:
### AI telemetry by source
| Source | Key fields | Security uses |
|---|---|---|
| **Gateway and API** | Identity (user, agent, key), client and source IP, endpoint, model requested, tokens in and out, latency, status and errors, rate-limit events | Credential misuse, abuse and extraction patterns, denial of wallet, shadow AI use |
| **Prompts and inputs** | Prompt text or a keyed hash, attachments, system prompt and template version, conversation and session IDs | Jailbreak and injection attempts, sensitive data sent to models |
| **Completions and outputs** | Output text or hash, refusals, finish reason, structured output validity, safety scores | Data leakage, harmful outputs, eroded safety behaviour |
| **Embeddings and retrieval** | Query, index and embedding model version, document IDs returned, scores, access-control filter applied | Poisoned or unexpected documents, access-control bypass, indirect injection sources |
| **Agents and tools** | Plan steps, tool name, arguments, results, approvals, delegated identity, MCP server | Excessive agency, hijacked agents, data exfiltration, runaway loops |
| **Guardrails and DLP** | Policy, detector, verdict, confidence, action taken (block, mask, flag) | Attack trends, false positives, control failures |
| **Platform and control plane** | Model registry changes, deployments, configuration and permission changes, key creation | Tampering, drift and privilege escalation (Module 5.1) |

### Getting telemetry out of AI systems
- **Gateways** give one consistent collection point for all model traffic, including traffic to external providers (Module 4.2).
- **Instrumentation libraries** in applications and agent frameworks emit traces and events. OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions for generative AI (still at development status in 2026) define standard names, such as `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, and agent operations such as `invoke_agent` and `execute_tool`. Capturing prompt and response **content is opt-in**, which supports privacy by default.
- **Provider logs** from hosted model platforms and cloud audit logs cover usage, administration and configuration changes.
- **Trace context:** propagate a trace ID across the gateway, agent, retrieval, model and tool calls (W3C Trace Context), so a whole request can be reconstructed.

### Practical choices
- Always record **versions**: model, system prompt, guardrail policy and index. Behaviour depends on them, and an investigation can’t reproduce an answer without them.
- Model outputs are often **non-deterministic**, so you can’t regenerate the same answer later. If an output may matter as evidence, keep it, or a keyed hash of it (Module 3.5).
- Decide **content capture by risk**: metadata always; content for high-risk applications, flagged sessions or a sample; full content only in a restricted store (Section 4).
- Watch **cost and volume**: AI telemetry is large. Filter, sample and tier storage, but never drop security-relevant events such as guardrail blocks, tool calls and administrative changes.

Is a stolen API key being used from a new country?

blocks.title: Telemetry questions
blocks.md: The best answers collect telemetry at **several layers** (gateway, agent, retrieval, model, tools), **join events with a trace ID**, and record **versions** of models, prompts and policies. Be wary of answers that log only the final output, or that log all content everywhere with no protection.

q.q: After an incident, investigators can see a customer assistant’s final answers, but can’t tell which documents it retrieved or which tools it called before answering. What should be added FIRST?
o: Longer retention for the existing logs of the assistant’s final answers
Retrieval and tool-call telemetry, linked to each request by a trace ID
A weekly report summarising the topics customers asked the assistant about
More detailed error messages shown to customers when the assistant fails
q.why: Investigators need the intermediate steps, joined to each request, to reconstruct what happened. Longer retention of the same logs, topic summaries and error messages don’t show what the assistant retrieved or did.

sections.title: Correlating AI events across SIEM, SOAR and threat intelligence

scenes.title: Joining the dots
scenes.sub: Correlating AI events across SIEM, SOAR and threat intelligence
scenes.say: A single AI event rarely proves an attack. A suspicious prompt, an unusual tool call and a large outbound message might each look harmless alone. Together, they tell a story. | This video covers how to correlate AI events across security information and event management, security orchestration and response, and threat intelligence.

scenes.title: An AI-aware detection pipeline
scenes.say: Here is an AI-aware detection pipeline. It starts with AI telemetry from gateways, agents, retrieval and tools. | Events are normalised into a common schema, then enriched: which person or agent is this, which application, which model version, and how sensitive is the data involved? | The SIEM correlates events using rules and analytics, raising alerts when patterns match. | A SOAR playbook then gathers more context, applies decision logic and takes action. | Responses include containment, such as disabling an agent or revoking a key, notifying the model owner, and opening a case. | Threat intelligence feeds the pipeline throughout, adding known bad indicators and attacker techniques to enrichment and detection.

scenes.title: Three weak signals, one incident

events.d: Agent paused, email held, case opened

scenes.say: Here is why correlation matters, in an incident that unfolds over three minutes. | At two minutes past ten, the injection detector flags a web page that a research agent retrieved. On its own, that is a low-severity alert, and detectors like this fire often. | A minute later, the same agent sends an email to a domain it has never contacted before. Unusual, but explainable. | The data loss prevention system finds customer records in that email. | Because all three events share the same trace identifier, the SIEM joins them into one critical incident: injected content, followed by exfiltration. | Within seconds, a SOAR playbook pauses the agent, holds the email and opens a case for the analyst.

scenes.title: SIEM, SOAR and threat intelligence
scenes.say: Each platform has a distinct job. | The SIEM collects and correlates events and raises alerts. SOAR automates response steps. Threat intelligence gathers and shares information about attackers. | For AI, the SIEM might detect an injection followed by data leaving. SOAR pauses the agent and revokes its key. Threat intelligence supplies known sources of model extraction or abuse. | Their outputs are alerts and incidents; actions and case records; and enrichment data and blocklists.

scenes.title: Threat intelligence for AI

items.d: IPs and networks behind extraction or abuse
Exposed AI provider keys and tokens
Hashes of backdoored or unsafe models

scenes.say: Threat intelligence for AI covers six kinds of information. | Infrastructure linked to model extraction, abuse or automated attacks. | Leaked credentials, such as AI provider keys exposed in code repositories. | Hashes of malicious or backdoored model files on public hubs. | Compromised AI libraries, packages and datasets. | Attacker techniques and campaigns, mapped to MITRE ATLAS, so detections can be aligned with real tactics. | And descriptions of known prompt injection and jailbreak styles, turned into detection signatures.

items: Normalise and enrich AI events with identity, asset and model context
Correlate weak signals by trace ID, identity and time
Automate safe responses with SOAR; humans for the rest
Feed and share AI threat intelligence, mapped to ATLAS
scenes.say: To recap. | Normalise AI events and enrich them with identity, asset and model context. | Correlate weak signals by trace identifier, identity and time, to reveal attacks that no single event shows. | Automate safe, reversible responses with SOAR, and keep humans in the loop for the rest. | And consume and share AI threat intelligence, mapped to MITRE ATLAS.

blocks.md:
### Making AI events usable in the SIEM
- **Normalise** events into the SIEM’s common schema, with consistent fields for identity, application, model, trace ID, action and outcome. Vendor-neutral schemas such as OCSF (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework) help.
- **Enrich** with context: the identity provider (who is this user or agent, and who sponsors it?), the asset inventory and model registry (which application, which model version, what risk tier?) and data classification (how sensitive is what was accessed?).
- **Correlate** using several techniques:

| Technique | AI example |
|---|---|
| **Single-event rule** | A guardrail blocks an attempt to retrieve a system prompt from a production assistant |
| **Threshold** | More than 200 refusals for one API key in ten minutes |
| **Sequence** | Injection detection, then a new tool or destination, then a DLP match, within one trace |
| **Cross-domain** | An AI agent’s token used from an IP address seen in threat intelligence |
| **Anomaly (UEBA)** | A service account’s query diversity suddenly rises, suggesting model extraction (Module 5.3) |

### SOAR for AI incidents
SOAR playbooks automate **enrichment** (look up the agent’s owner, recent changes and data access), **triage** (score severity using data sensitivity and blast radius) and **response**. Automate actions that are **safe and reversible**, such as pausing an agent, holding an outbound message, throttling a key or switching to a fallback model. Keep a **human approval** step for disruptive or irreversible actions, such as deleting data, rolling back a model for all customers or notifying regulators (Module 5.5).

### Threat intelligence pipelines
- **Sources:** commercial feeds, ISACs, CERTs, open-source vulnerability databases (CVE, OSV), model-hub security advisories, AI provider threat reports on misuse, and MITRE ATLAS case studies.
- **Formats:** share indicators and techniques with **STIX 2.1** over **TAXII 2.1**, so platforms can exchange them automatically.
- **Use:** block or flag known bad infrastructure at the gateway, add hashes of malicious models to registry and pipeline checks (Module 6.3), and turn reported techniques into detections and red-team scenarios (Module 6.4).
- **Share back:** report AI incidents and indicators through sector ISACs and partners. In the US, the 2025 AI Action Plan called for an AI Information Sharing and Analysis Center (AI-ISAC) led by DHS, which was still being developed in early 2026. CISA’s JCDC AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook (January 2025) describes voluntary sharing of AI incident information.

Map detections and incidents to **MITRE ATLAS** techniques (and ATT&CK for conventional steps). A shared vocabulary helps with coverage analysis ("which ATLAS techniques can we detect?"), reporting and intelligence sharing.

blocks.title: Correlation techniques
cards: Events in a set order within a time window or trace: for example, injection detected, then a new destination, then a DLP match.
A count crossing a limit: for example, hundreds of refusals for one key in minutes.
Adding context to events, such as the agent’s owner, the model’s risk tier or the data’s classification.
User and entity behaviour analytics: baselines per user, agent or key, with alerts on deviations.
A standard language for threat intelligence (STIX) and a protocol for exchanging it automatically (TAXII).

blocks.title: Correlation questions
blocks.md: Look for answers that **join weak signals** (by trace ID, identity and time), **enrich** them with model and data context, and **automate safe, reversible containment**. Isolated alerts reviewed one by one, or SOAR playbooks that take irreversible actions with no human approval, are weaker choices.

q.q: A SOC receives thousands of low-severity prompt injection alerts each week and has started ignoring them. Which improvement would BEST help it find the injections that matter?
o: Switch off the prompt injection detector, because its alerts are mostly noise
Correlate injection alerts with later tool calls, new destinations and DLP events
Ask the model provider to retrain its model so that it ignores injected text
Hire more analysts, so every individual alert can be reviewed by hand
q.why: Correlation raises the alerts where an injection was followed by risky actions, and leaves isolated detections at low priority. Disabling the detector loses signal, retraining isn’t a SOC control, and more analysts don’t fix the noise.

scenes.title: Logs you can stand behind
scenes.say: After an AI incident, logs become evidence, for the investigation, for regulators and sometimes for a court. Evidence is only useful if people can trust that it is complete and unaltered. | This video covers log integrity, and how to document evidence so it stands up to scrutiny.

scenes.title: Threats to AI logs

items.d: Logs leak the data they record

scenes.say: Six threats undermine AI logs. | Tampering and deletion: an attacker with access removes or edits the entries that show what they did. | Gaps: a collector fails, or a pipeline drops events under load, and nobody notices. | Clock drift: systems disagree about the time, so the timeline of an attack no longer lines up. | Log injection: input containing line breaks or control characters is written to logs unescaped, creating fake entries. With AI, any prompt or model output is untrusted input. | Exposure: logs full of prompts and outputs leak the very data they record. | And missing context: without model, prompt and configuration versions, nobody can explain why the system behaved as it did.

scenes.title: A tamper-evident log pipeline
scenes.say: Here is a log pipeline designed for integrity. At the source, every event carries a sequence number and a timestamp from a synchronised clock, in universal time. | A forwarder sends events over an encrypted channel, buffering and retrying until the collector acknowledges them, so nothing is silently lost. | The collector validates events and escapes untrusted text, so injected line breaks can’t forge entries. | Events land in immutable, write-once storage, with each batch chained to the hash of the one before. | Integrity checks verify the hashes and signed digests, and alert on gaps in sequence numbers or sources that go quiet. | And access is controlled: investigators get least privilege, administrators of the logged systems can’t alter the logs, and every access is itself logged.

scenes.title: Preventing and detecting log failures
scenes.say: Integrity needs both prevention and detection. | To prevent tampering, separate log administration from the systems being logged, and let sources write but never edit. To detect it, use hash chains and signed digests. | To prevent deletion, use write-once retention and legal holds. To detect attempts, alert on them. | To prevent gaps, use buffered delivery with acknowledgements. To detect them, monitor heartbeats and sequence numbers. | And to keep time trustworthy, synchronise every clock and record times in universal time, while monitoring for skew.

scenes.title: Documenting evidence
scenes.say: When logs become evidence, document them carefully. First, identify what is relevant: which systems, identities, traces and time ranges. | Collect it by exporting the records and calculating a cryptographic hash of each export. | Preserve the originals in immutable storage, under a legal hold if needed. | Record the chain of custody: who collected what, when, from where, with which hash, and every hand-off since. | Analyse working copies, never the originals, verifying hashes before you start. | And report findings that another analyst could repeat from the same evidence.

items: Protect logs from tampering, gaps, clock drift, injection and exposure
Sequence, escape, store immutably, verify and control access
Record model, prompt and configuration versions with events
Evidence: hash, preserve, record custody, analyse copies
scenes.say: To recap. | Protect AI logs against tampering, gaps, clock drift, injection and exposure. | Number events, escape untrusted text, store logs immutably, verify them continuously and control access. | Record model, prompt and configuration versions alongside events. | And handle evidence carefully: hash it, preserve it, record the chain of custody and analyse only copies.

blocks.md:
### Log integrity controls
- **Centralise quickly.** Forward logs off the source system as they are created, so an attacker who compromises an AI host or agent can’t erase the record.
- **Separate duties.** People who administer models, agents and platforms shouldn’t be able to change or delete their logs (Module 5.1).
- **Make logs tamper-evident.** Use write-once (WORM) storage or object lock, hash chaining or Merkle trees, and signed digests. Cloud services offer built-in options, such as AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation, which produces signed, hashed digest files. Signed syslog (RFC 5848) and trusted timestamps (RFC 3161) exist for the same purpose.
- **Detect gaps.** Use sequence numbers, heartbeats and volume baselines per source. A source that goes silent during an incident is itself a signal.
- **Synchronise time.** Use authenticated time sources, record timestamps in UTC with time zone information, and monitor clock skew.
- **Neutralise log injection.** Treat prompts, retrieved content, tool results and model outputs as untrusted. Encode or escape control characters and line breaks before writing them, and prefer structured formats such as JSON with proper escaping (CWE-117 describes this weakness).
- **Protect content.** Logs containing prompts and outputs are sensitive. Apply the privacy controls in Section 4 and Module 3.5.

### Logs as evidence
Evidence must be **relevant, authentic, complete and reliable**. Good practice for digital evidence is set out in ISO/IEC 27037 (identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence) and NIST SP 800-86 (integrating forensic techniques into incident response). For AI incidents:
- **Hash every export** (for example, SHA-256), record the hash in the evidence log, and verify it before each analysis.
- **Keep a chain of custody record:** item, source, collector, date and time, hash, storage location and each transfer.
- **Capture AI context:** model version and weights hash, system prompt and configuration versions, guardrail policies, retrieved document IDs, tool-call records and dataset snapshot references (Module 5.5 covers preserving these artefacts).
- **Remember non-determinism:** a model may not give the same answer twice, so the recorded output, or its keyed hash, is the evidence. You can’t simply regenerate it.
- **Apply legal holds** to suspend deletion when litigation or regulatory investigation is likely, overriding normal retention.
- **Document your methods:** which tools and queries were used, so findings can be reproduced.

blocks.title: Preparing AI logs as evidence
items: Scope the evidence
List the systems, identities, trace IDs and time ranges involved, including the model and agent versions in use at the time.
Export and hash
Export the relevant records from the immutable store, and calculate a hash for each export.
Preserve and hold
Store originals in write-once storage and apply a legal hold, so routine retention can’t delete them.
Record custody
Log who collected each item, when, from where, its hash, where it is stored, and every transfer.
Work on copies
Verify hashes, then analyse copies, recording the tools and queries used.

blocks.title: Log integrity questions
blocks.md: Strong answers make logs **tamper-evident** (WORM, hash chains, signed digests), **complete** (acknowledged delivery, gap detection), **time-consistent** and **separately administered**. For evidence, look for **hashing, preservation, chain of custody and analysis of copies**. Logs stored only on the compromised host are a classic weak answer.

q.q: During an investigation, analysts find that an AI agent’s logs were stored only on the agent’s own host, which the attacker controlled. What is the MOST important improvement?
o: Increase the size of the agent host’s local disk, so that logs are kept for longer
Forward logs in real time to a separately administered, immutable central store
Encrypt the logs on the agent host with a key stored on the same host
Ask the agent to summarise its own actions in a report at the end of each day
q.why: Logs held on a compromised host can be altered or deleted. Forwarding them immediately to separately administered, immutable storage preserves them. A bigger disk, a local key and self-reporting by the agent don’t protect against an attacker on the host.

blocks.title: See the threat, not the person

scenes.title: See the threat, not the person
scenes.say: AI telemetry is full of personal data. People paste customer records, health details and even passwords into prompts, and models repeat them in outputs. Security teams need to see attacks without exposing everyone’s private information. | This video covers privacy-preserving masking for AI telemetry.

scenes.title: Raw prompt and masked telemetry
rows: An API key pasted by mistake
scenes.say: Here is what masking does to one prompt. | A customer’s name becomes a consistent pseudonym, so analysts can still link her activity without seeing who she is. | Her email address gets its own token. | A card number keeps only its last four digits. | An API key that someone pasted by mistake is removed entirely, and the key is reported for rotation. | And the source address is generalised to its network range, which is still useful for spotting abuse.

scenes.title: Masking techniques

items.d: Reversible token; original in a vault

scenes.say: Six techniques do most of the work. | Redaction removes a value completely. It is right for secrets, which should never be stored. | Tokenisation replaces a value with a token, and keeps the original in a protected vault, so authorised people can reverse it. | Keyed hashing produces the same pseudonym every time for the same value, which keeps correlation working, but it can’t be reversed without the key. | Format-preserving encryption keeps the shape of the data, such as a sixteen-digit number, so downstream systems still work. | Generalisation turns exact values into ranges, such as an age band or a network range. | And differential privacy adds calibrated noise to aggregate statistics, so shared reports can’t reveal individuals.

scenes.title: Mask early, unmask rarely
scenes.say: The guiding principle is: mask early, unmask rarely. Raw prompts and outputs contain sensitive data. | Masking happens at collection, in the gateway or instrumentation library, before data leaves for storage or analysis. | Security analytics then works on pseudonyms. Because tokens are consistent, analysts can still follow one person or account across events. | When an investigation genuinely needs the real identity, an analyst raises a request tied to a case, stating the purpose, with an approver. | A separate team holds the token vault and keys, so the SOC can’t unmask data on its own. | And every unmasking is logged and reviewed.

scenes.title: Keeping masked telemetry useful
scenes.say: Masking must not blind the security team, so six practices keep it useful. | Use consistent tokens, so the same value always gets the same pseudonym and correlation still works. | Keep the fields security needs, such as internal identity identifiers and network ranges. | Mask every channel: not just prompts, but outputs, retrieved documents and tool results too. | Treat embeddings as sensitive. Research shows text can often be partly reconstructed from its embedding, so don’t ship raw vectors to the SIEM. | Test the masking regularly, because personal data detectors miss things, especially in free text and other languages. | And tier storage, keeping content for short periods and metadata for longer.

items: Mask personal data and secrets at collection, before storage
Pick the technique by need: redact, tokenise, hash, generalise
Unmask only through an approved, logged, separated process
Keep masked data useful: consistent tokens, every channel, tested
scenes.say: To recap. | Mask personal data and secrets at the point of collection, before they reach storage or analysis. | Choose the technique to fit the need: redact secrets, tokenise what may need reversing, hash for correlation and generalise for analysis. | Allow unmasking only through an approved, logged process, with keys held by a separate team. | And keep masked telemetry useful, with consistent tokens, coverage of every channel and regular testing.

blocks.md:
### Why mask AI telemetry?
Prompts, outputs, retrieved documents and tool results routinely contain personal data, confidential business information and secrets. Copying all of that into a SIEM creates a second, widely accessible store of sensitive data, which breaches **data minimisation** and **purpose limitation** (GDPR Article 5) and becomes an attractive target. Module 3.5 covered privacy-preserving audit trails; this section applies the same thinking to the SOC’s telemetry pipeline.

### Choosing a technique
| Technique | Reversible? | Keeps correlation? | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Redaction** | No | No | Secrets, passwords, full card numbers, special category data not needed for security |
| **Tokenisation** | Yes, through a vault | Yes | Customer and employee identifiers that investigators may need to resolve |
| **Keyed hashing (HMAC)** | No (without the key, only by guessing) | Yes | User IDs and email addresses for correlation; prompt and output fingerprints |
| **Format-preserving encryption** | Yes, with the key | Yes | Fields that downstream systems validate by format |
| **Generalisation** | No | Partly | IP addresses to network ranges, timestamps to hours, locations to regions |
| **Differential privacy** | No | No (aggregates only) | Usage and abuse statistics shared widely |

Pseudonymised data (tokens, keyed hashes) is **still personal data** under the GDPR, because it can be linked back to a person with additional information. Only properly anonymised data falls outside it.

### Designing the masking pipeline
- **Mask at the edge:** in the AI gateway, instrumentation library or log collector, before data is stored or forwarded. Masking later in the SIEM leaves raw copies in transit and in buffers.
- **Detect what to mask:** personal data detectors (named entity recognition plus patterns), **secret scanners** for keys and tokens, and custom detectors for business identifiers. When a secret is found, **remove it and trigger rotation**, because it has already been exposed to the AI system.
- **Cover every channel:** prompts, outputs, retrieved documents, tool arguments and results, agent memory and error messages.
- **Handle embeddings carefully:** **embedding inversion** research shows text can often be partly reconstructed from vectors, so treat them as sensitive. Log document or chunk IDs and similarity scores instead of raw vectors.
- **Separate the keys:** a different team (for example, privacy engineering) controls the token vault and hashing keys. Re-identification needs a case reference, a stated purpose and approval, and every request is logged.
- **Keep content selectively:** where full content is needed, such as for a flagged session or a high-risk application, keep it encrypted in a restricted store with short retention (Module 3.5).
- **Use built-in privacy defaults:** for example, OpenTelemetry’s generative AI conventions make prompt and response content capture opt-in.
- **Test regularly:** measure detector recall on realistic samples, including other languages and unusual formats, and fix gaps.

blocks.title: Which masking technique fits?
pairs: An API key pasted into a prompt
Redaction, plus rotating the key
Customer IDs investigators may need to resolve later
Tokenisation with a protected vault
Linking one user’s activity across events, without identity
Keyed hashing
Spotting abuse by network without exact addresses
Generalisation to network ranges
Monthly usage statistics shared across the company

blocks.title: Masking questions
blocks.md: The best answers **mask at collection**, use **consistent pseudonyms** so detection still works, **remove secrets entirely** (and rotate them), and allow **controlled, logged re-identification** by a separate key holder. "Collect everything raw and restrict SIEM access" and "collect nothing" are both weak.

q.q: A privacy review finds that full customer prompts, including health details, are copied into the SIEM, where 60 analysts can search them. The SOC says it needs the data to investigate abuse. What is the BEST approach?
o: Stop sending AI telemetry to the SIEM, so customer prompts are never exposed to analysts
Mask personal data at collection with consistent tokens; allow approved, logged re-identification
Keep sending full prompts, but ask every analyst to sign a confidentiality agreement
Move the full prompts to a separate SIEM that only the SOC manager is allowed to search
q.why: Masking at collection with consistent tokens keeps correlation and detection working, while re-identification stays possible for genuine cases under control. Stopping telemetry blinds the SOC, agreements don’t reduce exposure, and a separate SIEM still holds raw data.

scenes.title: What to watch in real time

layers.label: Behaviour

layers.label: Performance drift
layers.sub: Input and embedding shifts, quality and grounding scores

scenes.say: Real-time monitoring covers four layers. | Behaviour: safety classifier scores, refusal rates, jailbreak and injection detections, and personal data or secrets appearing in outputs. | Performance drift: shifts in the inputs and their embeddings, and falling quality or grounding scores. | Agent actions: which tools agents call, where they send data, which privileges they use, and whether they are stuck in loops. | And resources: tokens, cost, latency and errors, where sudden spikes can signal abuse or a runaway process.

scenes.title: An agent’s actions per minute
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative tool calls per minute by one support agent
scenes.say: Here is an illustrative support agent that normally makes around six tool calls a minute. | Its baseline sets an alert threshold well above normal variation. | At nine thirty-five, calls jump to more than thirty a minute, then fifty. That could be a loop, a flood of genuine work, or a hijacked agent working through a list of records. | The threshold breach triggers an automated pause within a minute, and an analyst reviews the trace before the agent resumes.

scenes.title: A real-time detection loop
scenes.say: A real-time detection loop has six parts. Every request, response and agent action becomes an event in a stream. | Online evaluators score events as they pass: fast classifiers for safety and data leakage on every event, and slower, model-based judges on a sample. | Detections combine those scores with rules and behavioural baselines. | When a high-risk detection fires, an automatic guard acts immediately and reversibly: throttling a key, pausing an agent or switching to a fallback. | The model owner and the security operations centre triage the alert, with the full trace in front of them. | And every alert feeds back into tuning: thresholds, rules and evaluators improve over time, reducing false positives.

scenes.title: Real-time and batch monitoring
scenes.say: Real-time monitoring complements batch monitoring rather than replacing it. | Real-time monitoring works in seconds or minutes. Batch monitoring works over hours or weeks. | Real time is best for stopping harm as it happens. Batch is best for trends, fairness and deeper evaluation. | For example, real time catches an agent emailing a domain it has never used. Batch measures accuracy each week once real outcomes are known. | Real time relies on lightweight classifiers and rules. Batch can afford heavier evaluation and human review.

items: Watch behaviour, drift, agent actions and resources
Baseline each agent and key; alert on deviations
Guard automatically and reversibly; humans triage
Combine real-time detection with batch evaluation
scenes.say: To recap. | Monitor behaviour, performance drift, agent actions and resource use in real time. | Baseline each agent, key and application, and alert on deviations. | Respond automatically, with reversible guards, while people triage and decide. | And combine real-time detection with batch evaluation for the full picture.

blocks.md:
### Real-time behaviour monitoring
- **Safety and policy:** run fast classifiers on inputs and outputs for toxicity, jailbreak and injection patterns, personal data and secrets (Module 4.4). Track rates per application and model version, with two-sided thresholds (Module 5.1).
- **Grounding and quality:** sample responses for model-based evaluation ("LLM as a judge") of groundedness, relevance and policy compliance. Judges are slower and costlier, so sample, and calibrate them against human review.
- **Refusal and block rates:** sudden changes in either direction can mean an attack campaign, a broken control or a model update that changed safety behaviour.

### Performance drift in real time
Module 1.3 introduced drift types, and Module 3.5 covered lifecycle monitoring. In operations:
- Track **input drift** over sliding windows: topic and language mix, prompt length, and **embedding drift** (for example, the distance between the current window’s average embedding and a baseline, or the share of inputs far from known clusters).
- Track **output drift**: response length, refusal rate, format failures and confidence.
- Use proxy signals while ground truth is delayed: user feedback, escalations to humans, corrections and complaints.
- Distinguish **drift** (the world changed) from **configuration change** (the system changed) by correlating with deployment and change records (Module 5.1).

### Monitoring agent actions
| Signal | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Action rate** per agent and task | Loops, runaway costs, automated abuse |
| **New tools or scopes** used for the first time | Over-delegation or hijacking (Module 4.6) |
| **New destinations** (domains, recipients, APIs) | Possible exfiltration after injection |
| **High-impact actions** (payments, deletions, permission changes) | Need approval and close review |
| **Data volume** read or sent | Bulk access or leakage |
| **Delegated identity** and approvals | Attribution and policy compliance (Module 4.5) |

### Alerts that work
- **Baselines per entity** (agent, key, application), because normal differs widely between them.
- **Severity from context:** data sensitivity, privileges and blast radius, not just the detector’s score.
- **Reversible automatic guards** for high-confidence, high-impact detections: throttle, pause, hold or fall back. These link to circuit breakers and kill switches (Module 5.7).
- **Dashboards per audience:** SOC (detections and incidents), model owners (behaviour and quality), finance (cost) and executives (risk posture).
- **Measure the monitoring itself:** time to detect, false positive rate, and coverage of the AI systems in the inventory.

blocks.title: The quiet weekend
blocks.md: A bank’s internal research agent can read market data, query a customer database and send email. Monitoring is reviewed in a weekly batch report. On Saturday night, after reading a web page containing hidden instructions, the agent queries 40,000 customer records and emails summaries to an external address. Nobody notices until Monday’s report.

q.q: Which monitoring improvement would MOST reduce the impact of a repeat incident?
o: Produce the batch report daily instead of weekly, and email it to the agent’s owner
Real-time alerts on new destinations and bulk data access, with an automatic pause
A policy reminding staff that agents mustn’t be left running at weekends
A larger language model for the agent, so it is less likely to follow injected text
q.why: Real-time detection of new destinations and bulk reads, with an automatic, reversible pause, stops the agent within minutes. A daily report still detects the problem hours later, a policy doesn’t monitor anything, and a larger model doesn’t reliably resist injection.

blocks.title: Real-time monitoring questions
blocks.md: Look for **per-entity baselines**, **context-based severity** and **automatic, reversible guards** for agents and keys, combined with **batch evaluation** for slower trends. Weekly reports, or monitoring that only measures model accuracy, are too slow for agents that act in seconds.

q.q: A team notices that its assistant’s answers have grown less grounded over two weeks. Deployment records show no changes. Which real-time signal would BEST show whether the cause is drift in user inputs?
o: The assistant’s average response latency, compared with its latency at launch
Embedding drift of incoming prompts against the baseline window
The total number of tokens the assistant used in each of the two weeks
The count of users who signed in to the assistant each day
q.why: Embedding drift measures whether the content of incoming prompts has moved away from what the assistant was built and tested for. Latency, token totals and sign-in counts don’t show what users are asking about.

quiz.q: Why should every AI telemetry event carry a shared trace ID?
o: So that events can be deleted together when the retention period ends
To join events from the gateway, agent, retrieval, model and tools for one request
To let the model provider bill each request to the correct customer account
To encrypt each event with a key derived from the request identifier
quiz.why: A trace ID lets analysts follow a single request through every layer, which is essential for reconstructing what an AI system did.

quiz.q: Which telemetry would BEST reveal that a RAG assistant returned a document the user wasn’t entitled to see?
o: Gateway logs showing the number of tokens sent and received in each request
Retrieval logs with document IDs and the access filter applied
Model serving logs showing the latency of each response
Billing records showing the monthly cost of the assistant
quiz.why: Only retrieval telemetry shows which documents came back for which user, and whether access filtering was applied.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record model and system prompt versions with AI events?
o: Versions are needed to work out the provider’s charges for each request
Behaviour depends on them, so investigators need them to explain outputs
Regulators require version numbers to be shown to users in every response
Version numbers make the logs smaller, because content can then be dropped
quiz.why: The same input can produce different behaviour under a different model or prompt version, so versions are part of the evidence.

quiz.q: What is the main role of SOAR in AI incident response?
o: Storing AI telemetry for long-term compliance and audit purposes
Running playbooks that enrich alerts and automate response actions
Training detection models on the organisation’s historical incidents
Sharing indicators with other organisations through industry groups
quiz.why: SOAR platforms orchestrate enrichment, triage and response steps, such as pausing an agent or revoking a key.

quiz.q: Why are sequence rules useful for detecting AI attacks?
o: They run faster than any other type of correlation rule in the SIEM
Weak signals in order, such as injection then exfiltration, reveal attacks
They remove the need to collect telemetry from AI agents and tools
They let analysts review every alert in the order it was received
quiz.why: Individually weak events become strong evidence when they occur in a meaningful order within one trace or time window.

quiz.q: What do STIX and TAXII provide?
o: A method for encrypting logs before they are forwarded to the SIEM platform
A standard format for threat intelligence, and a protocol to exchange it
A framework for scoring and classifying the severity of AI vulnerabilities
A certification scheme for security operations centre analysts
quiz.why: STIX describes threat intelligence in a standard structure, and TAXII exchanges it automatically between platforms and partners.

quiz.q: Why should AI logs be forwarded off the source system as they are created?
o: Local disks on AI servers are usually too small to hold all their telemetry
An attacker who compromises the host can’t then erase the record
Central storage is always cheaper than local storage
Model providers require logs to be stored in a central SIEM
quiz.why: Logs that stay on a compromised host can be altered or deleted, so they must leave it immediately for protected storage.

o: Adding extra logging statements to an application to improve its visibility
Untrusted input written unescaped, so crafted text forges log entries
Copying logs from one SIEM into another during a migration
Sending logs to the SIEM faster than it can process them
quiz.why: Prompts, outputs and tool results are untrusted input; escaping them before logging stops forged or corrupted entries (CWE-117).

quiz.q: Why should analysts work on copies of log evidence rather than the originals?
o: Copies are smaller, so analysis tools can process them more quickly
The originals stay unaltered, so findings can be verified against them
Original logs are encrypted, so most analysis tools can’t read them at all
Copies can be shared publicly without needing any approval
quiz.why: Preserved, hashed originals let anyone confirm that the evidence analysed is exactly what was collected.

quiz.q: Which masking technique keeps correlation working without allowing the value to be reversed?
o: Redaction, which removes the value entirely
Keyed hashing, which gives a consistent pseudonym
Tokenisation, which stores the original in a vault
Format-preserving encryption, which keeps the format
quiz.why: A keyed hash maps the same value to the same pseudonym every time, but can’t be reversed without the key. Tokenisation and encryption are reversible; redaction breaks correlation.

quiz.q: Why should masking happen at collection rather than inside the SIEM?
o: The SIEM can’t search data that has been masked by another system
Otherwise raw data sits in transit, buffers and storage before masking
Masking in the SIEM is prohibited by most data protection laws
Collection-time masking removes the need for any access controls
quiz.why: Masking at the edge means raw personal data and secrets never travel or rest in the analytics pipeline.

quiz.q: Why is a weekly report not enough to monitor AI agents?
o: Weekly reports can’t include charts of agent activity over time
Agents can cause serious harm in minutes, long before a weekly review
Regulators require AI agents to be monitored every hour of every day
Weekly reports are too expensive to produce for each agent
quiz.why: Agents act at machine speed, so detection and containment must work in seconds or minutes, with batch reports for trends.

o: A gradual increase in the size of the vector database over time
A shift in input embeddings away from a baseline, as user topics change
The loss of precision when embeddings are stored as smaller numbers
A change of embedding model made by the provider without telling its customers
quiz.why: Embedding drift shows that the content of inputs has moved away from what the system was built and tested for.

exam.q: An organisation’s AI gateway logs every request’s metadata, but its agents call internal APIs directly, and those calls aren’t logged. After a suspected data leak, investigators can’t tell what the agents did. What should be implemented FIRST?
o: A policy requiring agents to describe their actions in their final responses
Tool-call telemetry from the agent framework, linked to requests by trace ID
A second AI gateway in front of the first, to capture the same metadata twice
A monthly review of agent permissions by each agent’s business owner
exam.why: Tool-call telemetry, joined to requests, shows what agents actually did. Self-descriptions are unreliable, a second gateway sees the same traffic, and permission reviews don’t record actions.

exam.q: A company wants to capture full prompt and response content for all 40 of its AI applications, "in case it is ever needed". The privacy officer objects. What is the BEST compromise?
o: Capture full content for every application, but delete it after five years
Metadata for all; content by risk, flagged sessions or sample, in a restricted store
Capture no telemetry at all, so that there is no privacy risk from AI logging
Capture full content, but only for requests made by employees, not customers
exam.why: Metadata supports most detection; selective content in a restricted store supports investigations while respecting minimisation. Blanket capture, no capture and arbitrary splits by user type fail one goal or the other.

exam.q: A SOC wants to automate responses to AI alerts. Which action is MOST suitable for full automation without human approval?
o: Rolling back the model for all customers to a version from last year
Pausing an agent and holding its outbound message pending review
Deleting the training dataset that a poisoning alert refers to
Notifying the regulator that a serious AI incident has occurred
exam.why: Pausing and holding are safe and reversible, so they suit automation. Fleet-wide rollbacks, data deletion and regulatory notification are disruptive or irreversible and need human decisions.

exam.q: Threat intelligence reports that a set of IP addresses is systematically querying AI APIs across the financial sector to copy model behaviour. What should the SOC do with this intelligence?
o: Wait until the same addresses are actually seen attacking the organisation’s own systems
Add the indicators to gateway enrichment and detections, and hunt for past activity
Forward the report to all staff, asking them to watch for unusual AI behaviour
Ask the model provider whether it has seen the addresses, and do nothing else
exam.why: Operationalising intelligence means using it in detection and enrichment now, and hunting for earlier activity. Waiting, broadcasting to staff or relying on the provider leaves the organisation exposed.

exam.q: An attacker who gained administrator access to an AI platform deleted the platform’s local audit logs. Which control would BEST have preserved the evidence?
o: Daily email summaries of audit events sent to the platform administrators
Forwarding events in real time to a separately administered, write-once store
Encrypting the local audit logs with a key held by the platform administrators
Increasing the local audit log retention period from 30 days to one year
exam.why: Logs forwarded immediately to storage the attacker doesn’t control, and can’t modify, survive the compromise. Summaries, local encryption and longer local retention don’t.

exam.q: Investigators preparing AI logs for a legal case must show they haven’t been altered since collection. Which practice BEST supports this?
o: Storing the exported logs in a shared folder that only members of the legal team can see
Hashing each export, preserving originals, and recording the chain of custody
Printing the logs and asking the investigators to sign every page
Converting the logs into a summary report written by the lead investigator
exam.why: Hashes prove integrity, preserved originals allow verification, and a custody record shows who handled the evidence. Folder permissions, signatures on printouts and summaries don’t prove the data is unchanged.

exam.q: A SOC needs to track individual users’ activity across AI applications to detect abuse, but analysts mustn’t see customers’ identities. Which approach BEST meets both needs?
o: Remove all user identifiers from AI telemetry before it reaches the SIEM
Replace identifiers with consistent keyed-hash pseudonyms at collection
Show analysts full identities, but log every search they make in the SIEM
Ask customers to consent to their identities being visible to analysts
exam.why: Consistent pseudonyms preserve correlation without revealing identity. Removing identifiers breaks detection, logging searches doesn’t prevent exposure, and consent isn’t a substitute for minimisation.

exam.q: An employee pastes a production database password into an AI assistant’s prompt. The telemetry pipeline’s secret scanner detects it. What should happen?
o: Store the prompt as normal, because the SIEM is already access-controlled
Remove the secret from all telemetry and trigger rotation of the password
Tokenise the password, so investigators can recover it later if needed
Hash the password, so analysts can tell whether it is used again elsewhere
exam.why: Secrets should never be stored in telemetry, and once exposed to an AI system they must be rotated. Storing, tokenising or hashing them keeps an exposed credential in use.

exam.q: A bank’s customer chatbot shows a sudden doubling of refusals and a jump in jailbreak-detector hits from a small set of accounts. What is the MOST appropriate real-time response?
o: Wait for next week’s batch report to confirm the trend before taking any action
Throttle the accounts automatically, alert the SOC and investigate the pattern
Switch the chatbot off for all customers until the model can be retrained
Lower the jailbreak detector’s sensitivity, so it raises fewer alerts
exam.why: A targeted, reversible guard on the suspicious accounts, plus investigation, contains a likely attack campaign without affecting other customers. Waiting, a full shutdown or desensitising the detector are all poor responses.

exam.q: An AI agent that normally makes about 20 API calls an hour makes 3,000 in ten minutes, all to an internal HR system. What should the monitoring design have ensured?
o: That the agent’s owner reviews a summary of its activity at the end of each month
An alert from its per-agent baseline, with an automatic, reversible pause
That the HR system’s administrators are told to watch for unusual traffic
That the agent is rebuilt from scratch every week to reset its behaviour
exam.why: Per-agent baselines catch abnormal action rates quickly, and an automatic pause limits the damage while people investigate. Monthly reviews, informal watching and weekly rebuilds don’t detect or stop the activity.
